claims.text: Brittle behavior in compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can emerge through nucleation of nanoscale intragranular precipitates.
Nanoscale intragranular precipitates act as stress concentrators and initiate cracking.
The proposed intragranular precipitation mechanism is distinct from grain-boundary segregation associated with brittleness in conventional alloys.
The initial alloy is single-phase, compositionally complex, microstructurally uniform, and contains no significant precipitates.
Coupled high-temperature exposure and high-strain-rate loading will induce intragranular nanoscale precipitation.
The proposed test conditions are service-relevant and remain within operational limits for demanding engineering applications.
Minor local compositional fluctuations promote heterogeneous nucleation of nanoscale precipitates inside grains under high-temperature and high-strain-rate conditions.
The intragranular nanoscale precipitates gradually grow under the applied thermal and mechanical conditions.
The precipitates localize stress and deformation.
Stress localization around the precipitates reduces the alloy's ability to blunt or arrest crack propagation.
Reduced crack blunting or arrest causes brittle failure despite retention of an overall compositionally complex structure.
Relative to the baseline, the treated alloy will show earlier crack initiation.
Relative to the baseline, the treated alloy will show a marked reduction in toughness concurrent with emerging intragranular nanoscale precipitates.
Under ambient thermal and low-rate loading, the baseline alloy retains a homogeneous single-phase microstructure and high toughness.
Reduced toughness without detectable intragranular nanoscale precipitates would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Intragranular nanoscale precipitate formation without a corresponding toughness reduction would falsify the proposed mechanism.
